definitions.definition: A structural similarity between two different systems that shows they work in the same way, even if they are made of different things.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is isomorphic to the actual subway tracks because the connections between stations are the same, even though the map is paper and the tracks are metal.

definitions.definition: The study of the immune system, which is the body's defense against germs and other invaders.
definitions.example: Immunology explains how vaccines train your body to fight off diseases like the flu.

definitions.definition: The study of salvation, or how people are saved from sin and its consequences according to Christian belief.
definitions.example: Soteriology asks questions like 'How does Jesus's death save people?'

definitions.definition: The process of becoming more holy or morally pure, often seen as a gradual change in a believer's life.
definitions.example: Sanctification is like training to become a better person over time, not just deciding to be good once.

definitions.definition: A problem where you have to sort things into one of two groups, like 'yes' or 'no'.
definitions.example: A spam filter does binary classification: it decides if an email is spam or not spam.

definitions.definition: When a test or system says something is present when it actually isn't.
definitions.example: A fire alarm that goes off when there's no smoke is a false positive.

definitions.definition: When a test or system says something is absent when it actually is present.
definitions.example: A pregnancy test that says 'not pregnant' when the person is pregnant is a false negative.

definitions.definition: A condition where the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own healthy cells.
definitions.example: In type 1 diabetes, autoimmunity causes the immune system to attack the pancreas.

definitions.definition: A condition where the immune system is too weak to fight off infections properly.
definitions.example: HIV causes immunodeficiency, making it hard for the body to fight even a common cold.

definitions.definition: An overly strict focus on following rules, often leading to judging others harshly for minor things.
definitions.example: Legalism is like saying you can't be a good person unless you follow every single rule perfectly, even small ones.

definitions.definition: The belief that moral laws don't apply to believers, so they can do whatever they want without consequences.
definitions.example: Antinomianism is like thinking that because you're on a sports team, you don't have to follow any rules of the game.

definitions.definition: A graph that shows how well a classification system balances catching true threats (sensitivity) and avoiding false alarms (specificity).
definitions.example: A ROC curve can show if a medical test is good at finding cancer without too many false alarms.

definitions.definition: In testing, the ability to correctly identify true positives, or how good a system is at catching what it's looking for.
definitions.example: A sensitive smoke detector catches even tiny amounts of smoke.

definitions.definition: In testing, the ability to correctly identify true negatives, or how good a system is at avoiding false alarms.
definitions.example: A specific smoke detector doesn't go off when you're just cooking toast.

definitions.definition: A single number that measures the overall performance of a classification system, where 1.0 is perfect and 0.5 is random guessing.
definitions.example: An AUC of 0.9 means the system is very good at telling the two groups apart.

definitions.definition: A mathematical formula that calculates the total penalty for making mistakes, used to find the best balance between different types of errors.
definitions.example: A cost function for a factory might add up the cost of making too many products (waste) and the cost of making too few (lost sales).

definitions.definition: A strong feeling of guilt or certainty that something is wrong, often seen as a sign from God to change behavior.
definitions.example: Feeling bad after lying and deciding to tell the truth is an example of conviction.

definitions.definition: The ability to judge well, especially to tell the difference between right and wrong or good and evil.
definitions.example: Discernment is like having a good internal compass that helps you make wise choices.

definitions.definition: The state of being limited or having boundaries, especially in knowledge, power, or time.
definitions.example: Humans have finitude because we can't know everything or live forever.

definitions.definition: The process of making something as effective or perfect as possible, often by finding the best balance between competing factors.
definitions.example: Optimizing your study time means finding the right mix of subjects so you learn the most without getting exhausted.

definitions.definition: A system that can fail in two opposite ways, like being too aggressive or too passive, and health is the balance between them.
definitions.example: A thermostat has a dual-pathology: it can be too hot (overheating) or too cold (freezing), and the goal is to keep the temperature just right.

definitions.definition: A small organ in the chest where T-cells (a type of immune cell) learn to tell the difference between the body's own cells and invaders.
definitions.example: The thymus is like a training school for immune cells, teaching them who is friend and who is foe.

definitions.definition: The process of learning from a teacher or mentor to become a better follower of a faith, especially in Christianity.
definitions.example: Discipleship is like an apprenticeship where you learn how to live your faith from someone more experienced.

definitions.definition: The ability of the immune system to remember past infections and respond faster and stronger the next time.
definitions.example: Getting a vaccine gives you immune memory, so if you encounter the real virus, your body fights it off quickly.

definitions.definition: The ability to notice and identify regularities or repeated structures in data or experiences.
definitions.example: Recognizing that a certain cloud shape means rain is coming is a form of pattern recognition.

definitions.definition: Weakened or made less harmful, often used to describe a virus in a vaccine that is too weak to cause disease but still triggers an immune response.
definitions.example: An attenuated virus in a vaccine is like a practice opponent in sports that is strong enough to train you but not strong enough to hurt you.

definitions.definition: Killed or made completely inactive, so it cannot cause infection, but still used to train the immune system.
definitions.example: An inactivated virus in a vaccine is like a photo of a dangerous animal: it shows you what to look for but can't attack you.

definitions.definition: The quality of being firm and unwavering in your beliefs or actions, especially during difficult times.
definitions.example: Steadfastness is like a tree that stays standing even in a strong storm.

definitions.definition: When a problem gets so big that the whole system has to respond in a major way, not just a local part.
definitions.example: Systemic escalation is like when a small fire in one room spreads, and the entire building's fire sprinklers turn on.

definitions.definition: Relating to metabolism, the chemical processes in the body that keep you alive, like breaking down food for energy.
definitions.example: Running increases your metabolic rate, meaning your body burns more energy.

definitions.definition: Not welcoming or suitable for life or growth; harsh or unfavorable.
definitions.example: A desert is inhospitable because it's too hot and dry for most plants and animals.

definitions.definition: Special cells in bone marrow that can develop into all types of blood cells, including immune cells.
definitions.example: Hematopoietic stem cells are like the master builders that can become any kind of blood cell the body needs.

definitions.definition: The soft, spongy tissue inside bones where blood cells are made.
definitions.example: Bone marrow is like a factory inside your bones that produces red and white blood cells.

definitions.definition: In immunology, a state where the immune system does not attack something it normally would, either because it's harmless or because it's been trained not to.
definitions.example: The immune system has tolerance to food, so it doesn't attack the food you eat as if it were a germ.

definitions.definition: A state where immune cells become unresponsive to a specific invader, essentially going silent instead of fighting.
definitions.example: Anergy is like a guard who stops checking IDs because he's tired, letting anyone through.

definitions.definition: Molecules on the surface of germs or other substances that trigger an immune response.
definitions.example: Antigens are like name tags on germs that tell your immune system, 'I'm an invader, attack me!'

definitions.definition: A conscience that has been damaged or numbed by repeated sin, so it no longer feels guilt or recognizes wrongdoing.
definitions.example: A seared conscience is like a burn scar that has no feeling, so you can't tell when something is hurting you.

definitions.definition: The body's response to injury or infection, causing redness, swelling, heat, and pain, which helps healing but can be uncomfortable.
definitions.example: When you sprain your ankle, inflammation causes it to swell and feel warm as the body works to repair it.

definitions.definition: The natural shrinking and loss of function of the thymus as a person ages, reducing the production of new immune cells.
definitions.example: Thymic involution is like a school that gradually closes down as fewer new students enroll, relying more on older graduates.

definitions.definition: Wastes away or shrinks due to lack of use or aging.
definitions.example: A muscle that you never use atrophies and becomes smaller and weaker.

definitions.definition: Immature T-cells that have not yet encountered an invader and are ready to be trained to recognize specific threats.
definitions.example: Naive T-cells are like new recruits in an army who haven't seen combat yet but are ready to learn.

definitions.definition: A similarity in the way two different systems are organized or work, even if the systems themselves are different.
definitions.example: A tree's branching pattern has a structural parallel to a river's network of streams, even though one is wood and the other is water.

definitions.definition: A structural similarity between two different systems that shows they work in the same way, even if they are made of different things.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is isomorphic to the actual subway tracks because the connections between stations are the same, even though the map is paper and the tracks are metal.

definitions.definition: A religious ceremony or ritual that is believed to be a sign of God's grace, like baptism or communion.
definitions.example: In Christianity, baptism is a sacrament that symbolizes being cleansed from sin.

definitions.definition: The ability to produce a desired result; effectiveness.
definitions.example: The efficacy of a medicine is how well it actually cures the disease.

definitions.definition: A branch of mathematics that studies how information is measured, stored, and communicated, especially in the presence of noise.
definitions.example: Information theory explains how your phone can send a text message without errors, even if the signal is weak.

definitions.definition: A framework for making decisions under uncertainty, especially when you have to tell a real signal apart from background noise.
definitions.example: Signal detection theory is used in radar to decide if a blip is an enemy plane or just a flock of birds.

definitions.definition: The system of glands that produce hormones, which regulate things like growth, mood, and metabolism.
definitions.example: The endocrine system includes the thyroid gland, which controls how fast your body uses energy.

definitions.definition: A process where the output of a system influences its own input, either amplifying (positive feedback) or balancing (negative feedback) the effect.
definitions.example: A thermostat uses a feedback loop: when the room gets cold, it turns on the heat, and when it's warm enough, it turns off.

definitions.definition: Quantities that can take any value within a range, not just whole numbers, like height or temperature.
definitions.example: Your height is a continuous variable because it can be 150.2 cm, not just 150 or 151 cm.

definitions.definition: The idea that a lack of exposure to germs in early childhood can lead to a higher risk of allergies and autoimmune diseases.
definitions.example: The hygiene hypothesis suggests that kids who grow up on farms, with lots of exposure to animals and dirt, have fewer allergies.

definitions.definition: An updated version of the hygiene hypothesis, suggesting that exposure to certain harmless microbes (old friends) trains the immune system to not overreact.
definitions.example: The old friends hypothesis says that playing with pets early in life introduces friendly bacteria that help your immune system stay calm.

definitions.definition: Shows a relationship or connection between two things, where changes in one are associated with changes in the other.
definitions.example: Studying more correlates with getting better grades, but it doesn't necessarily mean studying causes better grades.

definitions.definition: When one thing increases, the other decreases, and vice versa.
definitions.example: The amount of time you spend watching TV and the amount of time you spend exercising are often inversely correlated.

definitions.definition: The act of weakening the immune system, either intentionally (with drugs) or due to disease.
definitions.example: Immunosuppression is used after an organ transplant to stop the immune system from attacking the new organ.

definitions.definition: Drugs that reduce the strength of the immune system, often used to treat autoimmune diseases or prevent transplant rejection.
definitions.example: Immunosuppressants are like turning down the volume on your immune system so it doesn't overreact.

definitions.definition: A situation where you have to give up one thing to get another, because you can't have both at the same time.
definitions.example: There's a tradeoff between speed and accuracy: you can finish a test quickly but make more mistakes, or go slowly and get more answers right.

definitions.definition: Existing as a natural and permanent part of something, not added from outside.
definitions.example: The risk of falling is inherent in riding a bike; it's part of the activity itself.

definitions.definition: Something that appears in data or results due to the method of measurement or analysis, not because it's real.
definitions.example: A smudge on a microscope slide is an artifact that might look like a cell but isn't really there.

definitions.definition: Lasting for a long time without weakening or breaking down.
definitions.example: A durable friendship lasts for years, even through arguments and distance.

definitions.definition: A repeated back-and-forth movement or change between two states or positions.
definitions.example: A pendulum swinging back and forth is an oscillation.

definitions.definition: Something that must happen because of the way a system is built, not by chance or choice.
definitions.example: In a car, the wheels must turn for it to move; that's a structural necessity.

definitions.definition: From the beginning or from scratch; starting anew each time.
definitions.example: If you write an essay de novo, you don't use any previous drafts; you start from a blank page.

definitions.definition: The number of meaningful links or similarities between two systems, used to judge how likely the similarity is due to chance.
definitions.example: If two puzzles have many pieces that fit together perfectly, the connection density is high, meaning they probably go together on purpose.

definitions.definition: A strong, detailed similarity in the way two different systems are organized, showing they share the same underlying pattern.
definitions.example: A computer's file system and a library's book catalog have a structural isomorphism: both organize items into folders/categories and allow you to search for them.
